claim: In mice, sciatic nerve invasion by blood vessels begins around embryonic day 16 and continues until birth.
source: We found, in mice, that the sciatic nerve invasion by blood vessels begins around embryonic day 16 and continues until birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1, which displays immunofluorescence staining of sciatic nerves at different developmental stages showing the progression of blood vessel invasion.

claim: Intra-nervous blood vessel density significantly decreases during post-natal period, starting from P10.
source: Interestingly, intra-nervous blood vessel density significantly decreases during post-natal period, starting from P10.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3D showing CD31 density measurements across developmental stages.

claim: Netrin-1 promotes nerve invasion by blood vessels via the endothelial receptor UNC5B during embryogenesis.
source: We show that, while the axon guidance molecule Netrin-1 promotes nerve invasion by blood vessels via the endothelial receptor UNC5B during embryogenesis, myelinated Schwann cells negatively control intra-nervous vascularization during post-natal period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using Ntn1lacZ/lacZ mutant mice and anti-UNC5B blocking antibodies, showing reduced vascularization (Figure 6).

claim: Myelinated Schwann cells negatively control intra-nervous vascularization during post-natal period.
source: We show that, while the axon guidance molecule Netrin-1 promotes nerve invasion by blood vessels via the endothelial receptor UNC5B during embryogenesis, myelinated Schwann cells negatively control intra-nervous vascularization during post-natal period.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments using Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ and Krox20Cre/Fl mice showing hypervascularization when Schwann cells or myelin are absent (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: At E15.5, no blood vessels were observed inside or surrounding the sciatic nerve.
source: At E15.5, the extrinsic artery of the primitive sciatic nerve is aligned with axons (TUJ-1 staining). However, no blood vessels were observed inside or surrounding the nerve (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At E16, new blood vessels emerge from the aligned extrinsic artery to form a peri-nervous vascular plexus.
source: At E16, we noticed new blood vessels emerging from the aligned extrinsic artery to form a peri-nervous vascular plexus (Figure 1B, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At E16, numerous angiogenic sprouts invade the inside part of the immature nerve in the proximal region.
source: Developing from this latter, numerous angiogenic sprouts invade the inside part of the immature nerve, starting to form the intra-nervous vascular network (INV) as observed in the optical section of the proximal part of the nerve (Figure 1C, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by optical section imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At E16, no blood vessels were found inside the distal part of the nerve.
source: However, at E16, in the distal part no blood vessels were found inside the nerve (Figure 1D), suggesting a proximo-distal gradient of nerve invasion by blood vessels.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a proximo-distal gradient of nerve invasion by blood vessels at E16.
source: However, at E16, in the distal part no blood vessels were found inside the nerve (Figure 1D), suggesting a proximo-distal gradient of nerve invasion by blood vessels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that blood vessels are present in the proximal but not distal part of the nerve at E16.

claim: At E19, many angiogenic sprouts are found inside a dense vascular plexus, indicating ongoing angiogenesis.
source: Later, at E19, many angiogenic sprouts are still found inside a dense vascular plexus, implying that angiogenesis is still ongoing (Figure 1G and H, arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing angiogenic sprouts in Figure 1G and H.

claim: At birth (P0), angiogenic sprouts are found inside the nerve.
source: At birth (P0) (Figure 1I), angiogenic sprouts were also found inside the nerve (Figure 1J, arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: At P2 and P5, very few angiogenic sprouts were observed.
source: Finally, at P2 and P5, very few angiogenic sprouts were observed (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: The number of angiogenic sprouts per mm2 significantly decreases throughout development, between E19 and P0 and between P0 and P2.
source: We found that the number of angiogenic sprouts per mm2 significantly decreases throughout development, between E19 and P0 and between P0 and P2, to reach a number of almost zero angiogenic sprout at P5 (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1M with statistical significance indicated.

claim: At P0, endothelial cells of arterioles specifically express the protein connexin-40 (Cx-40).
source: Endothelial cells of arterioles specifically express the protein connexin-40 (Cx-40), as observed at P0 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At P5, endothelial cells expressing Cx-40 in an isolated manner were visible, suggesting that new arterial branches undergo differentiation inside the nerve.
source: Pre-existing blood vessels of the INV also undergo arterial differentiation, as observed in sciatic nerve at P5. Endothelial cells expressing Cx-40 in an isolated manner were visible (Figure 2C, arrowheads), suggesting that new arterial branches undergo differentiation inside the nerve.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C and is inferred from the pattern of Cx-40 expression.

claim: The Cx-40/CD31 integrated density was higher in nerves at P0 compared to P5.
source: The Cx-40/CD31 integrated density was higher in nerves at P0 compared to P5 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At P0, numerous endothelial cells of the INV are already covered by pericytes.
source: At P0, numerous endothelial cells of the INV are already covered by pericytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Pericytes at P0 have an elongated shape and their coverage is relatively sparse compared to pericytes observed at P10.
source: These pericytes at P0 have an elongated shape and their coverage is relatively sparse compared to the pericytes observed at P10 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative imaging data shown in Figure 2E and 2G.

claim: Blood vessel coverage by pericytes NG2+ cells increases between P5 and P10.
source: Blood vessel coverage by pericytes NG2+ cells increase between P5 and P10 (Figure 2H) suggesting maturation and stabilization of the new blood vessels whereas angiogenesis is almost stopped.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The caliber of the sciatic nerve gradually increases during post-natal development by a factor of 10 from P0 to young adulthood.
source: As expected, the caliber of the sciatic nerve gradually increases during post-natal development by a factor of 10 from P0 to young adulthood (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The intra-nervous CD31-positive area covers around 8% of the nerve at P0.
source: The intra-nervous CD31-positive area covers around 8% of the nerve at P0.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CD31 immunoreactivity shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The intra-nervous CD31-positive area decreases significantly at P10 to reach a stable coverage of approximately 2% of the nerve.
source: This value decreases after birth significantly at P10, to reach a stable coverage of approximately 2% of the nerve, and does not change later at young adult stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance indicated.

claim: The decrease in INV rate correlates with the myelination period during the 2 weeks after birth.
source: Interestingly, this decrease in INV rate correlates with the myelination period during the 2 weeks after birth (gray box, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal correlation between decreased vascularization and the known timing of myelination.

claim: The majority of cells within the sciatic nerve are Schwann cells (∼70%).
source: As nerve vascularization density decreases during post-natal development and while myelin is produced and since the majority of cells within the sciatic nerve are SC (∼70%) (Stierli et al., 2018), we wondered if myelinating SC could affect nerve vascularization.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stierli et al., 2018.

claim: Schwann cells promote endothelial cell migration in vitro.
source: It has been previously described that SC promote endothelial cells migration in vitro (Ramos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramos et al., 2015.

claim: At E19, there is significantly less Schwann cells (expressing SOX10) in sciatic nerves from Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mutant mice.
source: In fact, at E19, there is significantly less SC (expressing SOX10) in sciatic nerves from Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mutant mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, A', B and B')
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At P5, there are less myelinating Schwann cells (normally expressing S100β protein) in Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mutant mice.
source: and at P5, less myelinating SC (normally expressing S100β protein) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and C').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and C'.

claim: The sciatic nerves of Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mice were thinner as compared to Wnt1-Cre control littermates at P5.
source: As expected, the sciatic nerves of Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mice were thinner as compared to Wnt1-Cre control littermates (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4A, B, and F.

claim: The INV network is disrupted, denser, and more anastomotic in Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mice, resembling embryonic immature plexus.
source: Furthermore, the INV network is disrupted, denser, and more anastomotic, resembling embryonic immature plexus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C and quantitative analysis in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Sciatic nerves from Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mutant pups display an increased total length of blood vessel network compared to control littermates at P5.
source: Sciatic nerves from mutant pups display an increased total length of blood vessel network (Figure 4G) with more branches (Figure 4H) as compared to the control littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Sciatic nerves from Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mutant pups have more blood vessel branches compared to control littermates at P5.
source: Sciatic nerves from mutant pups display an increased total length of blood vessel network (Figure 4G) with more branches (Figure 4H) as compared to the control littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: At P0, nerve size is not different between Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mice and control mice, whereas vasculature is disrupted and more dense in the sciatic nerves of Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+ mice.
source: At this stage, nerve size is not different between the two groups, whereas vasculature is disrupted and more dense in the sciatic nerves of Wnt1-Cre;Krox20GFP(DT)/+mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B'.

claim: Myelinating Schwann cells could control INV development and maturation by negatively controlling angiogenesis.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that myelinating SC could control INV development and maturation probably by negatively controlling angiogenesis in order to ensure a proper amount of blood vessels inside the nerve.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing hypervascularization when Schwann cells are ablated.

claim: In Krox20Cre/Fl mice, Krox20 from the floxed allele is expressed until enough Cre recombinase accumulates resulting in the delayed inactivation of the Krox20 gene in myelinating Schwann cells.
source: As previously described, in these mice, Krox20 from the floxed allele is expressed until enough Cre recombinase accumulates resulting in the delayed inactivation of the Krox20 gene in myelinating SC (Decker et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Decker et al., 2006.

claim: Krox20 inactivation blocks Schwann cells at an early stage of their differentiation and progressively prevents the formation of myelin sheaths.
source: Krox20 inactivation blocks SC at an early stage of their differentiation, progressively prevents the formation of myelin sheaths (Figure 5A) and this phenotype is maintained through the 3 weeks of survival observed for those mice (Decker et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Decker et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Sciatic nerves of Krox20Cre/Fl mutant mice appear to be more densely vascularized compared to control littermates at P19.
source: Interestingly, sciatic nerves of mutant mice appear to be more densely vascularized compared to control littermates (Figure 5B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B and B'.

claim: Sciatic nerves from Krox20Cre/Fl mice have higher blood vessel total length compared to control mice at P19.
source: As compared to control mice, quantifications revealed a similar nerve size (Figure 5D) but higher blood vessel total length (Figure 5E) and higher number of branching points in mutant's sciatic nerves (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Sciatic nerves from Krox20Cre/Fl mice have higher number of branching points compared to control mice at P19.
source: As compared to control mice, quantifications revealed a similar nerve size (Figure 5D) but higher blood vessel total length (Figure 5E) and higher number of branching points in mutant's sciatic nerves (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At P18, in sciatic nerves from control mice, claudin-5 staining colocalized with CD31 staining in almost all blood vessels.
source: At P18, in sciatic nerves from control mice, claudin-5 staining colocalized with CD31 staining in almost all blood vessels (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In sciatic nerves from Krox20Cre/Fl mice at P18, claudin-5 is poorly expressed by endothelial cells as almost all blood vessels branches are claudin-5 negative.
source: In sciatic nerves from Krox20Cre/Fl mice, claudin-5 is poorly expressed by endothelial cells as almost all blood vessels branches are claudin-5 negative (Figure 5G', arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G'.

claim: Myelin sheath controls sciatic nerve vascularization by inhibiting angiogenesis and by limiting vascular rate and maturation.
source: Altogether, those data suggest that myelin sheath controls sciatic nerve vascularization by inhibiting angiogenesis and by limiting vascular rate and maturation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing hypervascularization and reduced claudin-5 expression when myelin is absent.

claim: The number of proliferating cells expressing Ki67 is considerably higher in the unmyelinated sciatic nerves from Krox20Cre/Fl mice.
source: Interestingly, the number of proliferating cells expressing Ki67 is considerably higher in the unmyelinated sciatic nerves (Figure 5H,H',I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 5H, H', and I.

claim: The proliferating cells in Krox20Cre/Fl sciatic nerves are Schwann cells, as they specifically express the protein SOX10.
source: As reported before (Topilko et al., 1994), these proliferating cells are SC, as they specifically express the protein SOX10 (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5J and a citation to Topilko et al., 1994.

claim: At E17, β-galactosidase expression (reporting Netrin-1 expression) was found inside and surrounding the sciatic nerve.
source: At E17, a stage during which new blood vessels are attracted into the endoneurial part of the nerve, we noticed that β-galactosidase expression was found inside and surrounding the nerve (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and B'.

claim: At P2, β-galactosidase activity, reporting Netrin-1 expression, was found close to blood vessels.
source: At P2, β-galactosidase activity, reporting Netrin-1 expression, was found close to blood vessels, in areas compatible with a potential role of Netrin-1 in endothelial cell guidance (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ntn1 is expressed by epineurial and perineurial cells and proliferating fibroblast-like cells.
source: Single cell transcriptomic analysis of the different cell types constituting sciatic nerves showed that Ntn1 is in fact expressed by epineurial and perineurial cells and proliferating fibroblast-like cells (Gerber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerber et al., 2021.

claim: At P0, expression of β-galactosidase (reporting Netrin-1 expression) was found at the level of FAP+ cells (fibroblast activation protein) located at the epi-perineurial cell layer.
source: We confirmed at P0 that expression of β-galactosidase (reporting Netrin-1 expression) was found at the level of FAP+ cells (fibroblast activation protein) located at the epi-perineurial cell layer (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ntn1 mRNA is expressed by epi-perineural cells expressing Fap mRNA.
source: Using FISH (fluorescent in situ hybridization), we also found Ntn1 mRNA expressed by epi-perineural cells expressing Fap mRNA (Figure 6C, C' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 6C, C' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Nerves from Ntn1lacZ/lacZ embryos are less vascularized compared to control embryos at E17.5.
source: Whereas there is no difference in terms of nerve area (Figure 6D), we found that nerves from mutant embryos are less vascularized as compared to control embryos (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dissected nerves shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Sciatic nerves of Ntn1lacZ/lacZ embryos had the same area as control littermates at E17.5.
source: We also found that, whereas sciatic nerves of Ntn1lacZ/lacZ embryos had the same area as control littermates (Figure 6H), they were less vascularized.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cleared limbs shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Sciatic nerves of Ntn1lacZ/lacZ embryos were less vascularized than control littermates at E17.5 as confirmed by analysis of cleared limbs.
source: We also found that, whereas sciatic nerves of Ntn1lacZ/lacZ embryos had the same area as control littermates (Figure 6H), they were less vascularized. This was confirmed by quantification of CD31-positive area density inside the nerve (Figure 6I), with a similar ratio and in agreement with our findings on dissected nerves.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CD31-positive area density shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The sural nerve has no blood vessels at E17.5 in both Ntn1lacZ/lacZ and Ntn1+/+ mice.
source: Interestingly, when we looked at the sural nerve, a purely sensory branch of the sciatic nerve (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), we found no blood vessels at this stage in neither Ntn1lacZ/lacZ nor Ntn1+/+ mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and B'.

claim: Phrenic nerve, intercostal (mixed motor/sensory), and cutaneous (purely sensory nerve) were devoid of INV at peri-natal stages (E17.5-P2).
source: Other nerve types such as phrenic nerve, intercostal (mixed motor/sensory), or cutaneous (purely sensory nerve) were also devoid of INV at peri-natal stages (E17.5-P2) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C to E'').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C to E''.

claim: Endothelial cells from sciatic nerves at P2 do not express dcc mRNA.
source: We found that endothelial cells from INV do not express dcc mRNA, whereas neogenin1 is weakly expressed and unc5b is highly expressed (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from isolated endothelial cells shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Endothelial cells from sciatic nerves at P2 weakly express neogenin1 mRNA.
source: We found that endothelial cells from INV do not express dcc mRNA, whereas neogenin1 is weakly expressed and unc5b is highly expressed (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from isolated endothelial cells shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Endothelial cells from sciatic nerves at P2 highly express unc5b mRNA.
source: We found that endothelial cells from INV do not express dcc mRNA, whereas neogenin1 is weakly expressed and unc5b is highly expressed (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from isolated endothelial cells shown in Figure 6J.

claim: unc5b is expressed by endothelial cells of INV of sciatic nerve at P0.
source: Using FISH technique, we established that unc5b is indeed expressed by endothelial cells of INV of sciatic nerve at P0 (Figure 6K and K', Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 6K and K', Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: UNC5B protein is expressed by endothelial cells of INV at P0.
source: Finally, we also confirmed that UNC5B protein is expressed by those endothelial cells (Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: INV density is significantly lower in sciatic nerves from pups injected with anti-UNC5B compared to pups injected with vehicle.
source: We found that INV density is significantly lower in sciatic nerves from pups injected with anti-UNC5B compared to pups injected with the vehicle (Figure 6M).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6M.

claim: Netrin-1, expressed at the level of epi-perineurial layer, and its receptor UNC5B, expressed by endothelial cells, are likely to be regulating the attraction and angiogenesis of the blood vessels inside the sciatic nerve around birth.
source: These data suggest that Netrin-1, expressed at the level of epi-perineurial layer, and its receptor UNC5B, expressed by endothelial cells, are likely to be regulating the attraction and angiogenesis of the blood vessels inside the sciatic nerve around birth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing Netrin-1 and UNC5B expression patterns and the effects of their loss of function.

claim: INV appears relatively late during embryonic development, around E16, as compared to the vasculature of the CNS which begins around E9.5.
source: We find that INV appears relatively late during embryonic development, around E16, as compared to the vasculature of the CNS which begins around E9.5 (Tata et al., 2015; Himmels et al., 2017) to ensure adequate delivery of oxygen and nutrients to neural progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from this study and citations to Tata et al., 2015 and Himmels et al., 2017.

claim: E16 in the mouse embryo represents a turning point for the peripheral nervous system as Schwann cell precursors acquire an immature phenotype.
source: E16 in the mouse embryo represents a turning point for the peripheral nervous system (PNS) as SCP acquire an immature phenotype (Jessen and Mirsky, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jessen and Mirsky, 2019.

claim: Angiogenesis continues until P10 in the CNS in mice.
source: This suggests that nerves reach their optimal blood vessel density around P10 similarly to the CNS in which angiogenesis continues until P10 in mice (Harb et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harb et al., 2013.

claim: Schwann cells are required for arterial differentiation in the skin of mouse embryos.
source: Mukouyama and colleagues have shown that SC are required for arterial differentiation in the skin of mouse embryos (Mukouyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mukouyama et al., 2002.

claim: Schwann cell-conditioned medium inhibits endothelial cell proliferation and migration in vitro.
source: Another study has suggested that SC-conditioned medium inhibits endothelial cell proliferation and migration in vitro (Huang et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2000.

claim: Oligodendrocytes promote angiogenesis and endothelial cell proliferation in the white matter.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that, oligodendrocytes promote angiogenesis and endothelial cell proliferation in the white matter (Yuen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yuen et al., 2014.

claim: Netrin-1 stimulates angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo in the retina.
source: It has been shown that Netrin-1 stimulates angiogenesis in vitro and also in vivo, in the retina (Park et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2004.

claim: Blood vessels inside the nerve are used by Schwann cells to direct migration during nerve regeneration.
source: It has been shown that blood vessels inside the nerve are used by SC to direct this migration (Cattin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cattin et al., 2015.

claim: Nerve grafts appear to be more efficient when their vascularization is preserved, allowing better regeneration.
source: Moreover, nerve grafts appears to be more efficient when their vascularization is preserved, allowing a better regeneration (D′Arpa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to D'Arpa et al., 2015.

claim: At E15, arteries and nerves start to be aligned in the skin.
source: At this stage arteries and nerves start to be aligned in the skin (Mukouyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mukouyama et al., 2002.

claim: Pericytes are critical for angiogenesis.
source: Some of these cells cover new blood vessel branching (Figure 2F) as it has been already reported that pericytes are critical for angiogenesis (Bergers and Song, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bergers and Song, 2005.

claim: Pericytes are important for maintenance of the blood-nerve barrier and are able to contract to change the capillary diameter.
source: Moreover, pericytes, expressing the protein NG2 and covering endothelial cells, are important for maintenance of the blood-nerve barrier and are able to contract to change the capillary diameter (Bergers and Song, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bergers and Song, 2005.

claim: Claudin-5 is a tight junction protein important for the acquisition of barrier property in blood vessels.
source: Endothelial cells composing the INV express claudin-5, a tight junction protein, important for the acquisition of a barrier property (Peltonen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peltonen et al., 2013.

claim: Activation of genes controlling myelination, such as KROX20, induces the arrest of the proliferation state of Schwann cells in favor of differentiation and production of myelin sheath.
source: Indeed, activation of the genes controlling myelination, such as KROX20, induces the arrest of the proliferation state of SC in favor of differentiation and production of myelin sheath (Salzer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salzer, 2015.

claim: Netrin-1 is a guidance molecule known to control axonal guidance and angiogenesis.
source: Netrin-1 is a guidance molecule known to control axonal guidance and also angiogenesis (Boyer and Gupton, 2018; Bradford et al., 2009; Park et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer and Gupton, 2018; Bradford et al., 2009; Park et al., 2004.

claim: Netrin-1 can be implicated in nerve regeneration, stimulating axonal and blood vessel regrowth.
source: Studies have shown that it can also be implicated in nerve regeneration, stimulating axonal and blood vessels regrowth (Dun and Parkinson, 2017; Madison et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dun and Parkinson, 2017; Madison et al., 2000.

claim: The role of Netrin-1 regarding angiogenesis is dual, depending on the receptor it binds to.
source: The role of Netrin-1 regarding angiogenesis remains controversial, and seems to be dual, as it is in axon guidance, depending on the receptor it binds to Yang et al., 2007.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2007.

claim: Ntn1–/– mice die around birth.
source: As Ntn1–/– mice die around birth (Serafini et al., 1996), we analyzed entire sciatic nerves of Ntn1lacZ/lacZ knock-in embryos at E16, before INV onset (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and E').
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Serafini et al., 1996.

claim: The transcription factor KROX20, expressed by immature Schwann cells, represents the master regulator of myelin genes and controls myelination formation and maintenance.
source: The transcription factor KROX20, expressed by immature SC, represents the master regulator of myelin genes and thus controls myelination formation and maintenance (Topilko et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Topilko et al., 1994.

claim: Schwann cell precursors derive from neural crest cells and migrate from the neural tube around embryonic day E10.5 to contact axons.
source: Simultaneously, SC precursors (SCP) derive from the neural crest cells and migrate from the neural tube around embryonic day E10.5 to contact axons and differentiate into immature SC (iSC) around E15/E16 (Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008.

claim: Schwann cell precursors differentiate into immature Schwann cells around E15/E16.
source: Simultaneously, SC precursors (SCP) derive from the neural crest cells and migrate from the neural tube around embryonic day E10.5 to contact axons and differentiate into immature SC (iSC) around E15/E16 (Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008.

claim: Around birth, Schwann cells differentiate into either myelinating or non-myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Finally, around birth they differentiate into either myelinating or non-myelinating SC.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Schwann cell development.

claim: In rodents, myelination is progressive, starts around birth, and lasts during about 2 weeks.
source: In rodents, myelination is progressive, starts around birth, and lasts during about 2 weeks (Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Woodhoo and Sommer, 2008.

claim: Schwann cells are necessary to ensure axonal survival during development and in regeneration.
source: SC are necessary to ensure axonal survival during development and also in regeneration (Jessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jessen et al., 2015.

claim: Adult nerves are stable structures, with nerve fibers surrounded and protected by three layers of connective tissues: the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium.
source: Adult nerves are stable structures, with nerve fibers surrounded and protected by three layers of connective tissues: the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium (Kaplan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaplan et al., 2009.

claim: A dense network called the vasa nervorum ensures the maintenance of proper nerve homeostasis.
source: Indeed, a dense network called the vasa nervorum ensures the maintenance of proper nerve homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The organization of the vasa nervorum vascular system has been previously described.
source: The organization of this vascular system has been previously described (Boissaud-Cooke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boissaud-Cooke et al., 2015.

claim: Blood vessels are found within the three connective tissues of nerves, all along the nerve length, forming the peri- and intra-nervous vascular system.
source: In fact, blood vessels are found within the three connective tissues, all along the nerve length, forming the peri- and intra (INV)-nervous vascular system.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Blood vessels in nerves are composed of a single layer of endothelial cells surrounded by mural cells: smooth muscle cells and pericytes.
source: They are composed of a single layer of endothelial cells surrounded by mural cells: the SMC and pericytes allowing the contraction of the blood vessel to adapt the blood flow.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about blood vessel structure.

claim: During early stages of embryogenesis, by a process called vasculogenesis, a part of the mesoderm differentiates into endothelial cells, forms a lumen, and deposits a basal lamina to create a vascular plexus de novo.
source: During early stages of embryogenesis, by a process called vasculogenesis, a part of the mesoderm differentiates into endothelial cells, forms a lumen, and deposits a basal lamina to create a vascular plexus de novo.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about vascular development.

claim: During development and in the adult, new blood vessels are formed from pre-existing ones by a process called angiogenesis.
source: During development and in the adult, new blood vessels are formed from pre-existing ones by a process called angiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about vascular development.

claim: Angiogenesis involves specialized endothelial cells named tip cells.
source: This mechanism involves specialized endothelial cells named tip cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about angiogenesis.

claim: Tip cells can sense the microenvironment and respond to guidance cues to lead the angiogenic sprout.
source: Thanks to the expression of specific receptors, tip cells can sense the microenvironment, and respond to guidance cues to lead the angiogenic sprout.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about tip cell function.

claim: Formation of vascular plexus and its maturation into a dense network of blood vessels is one of the most important mechanisms during embryonic and post-natal development in vertebrates.
source: Formation of vascular plexus and its maturation into a dense network of blood vessels is one of the most important mechanisms during embryonic and post-natal development in vertebrates (Kolte et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kolte et al., 2015.

claim: The vascular network transports oxygen and nutrients and eliminates waste products, all critical for organ survival and cellular homeostasis.
source: Among numerous physiological tasks, the vascular network transports oxygen and nutrients and eliminates waste products, all critical for organ survival and cellular homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about vascular function.

claim: Peripheral nerves connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
source: Peripheral nerves, connecting the central nervous system (CNS) to the rest of the body, are composed of axons covered by myelinating and non-myelinating Schwann cells (SC).
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Peripheral nerves are composed of axons covered by myelinating and non-myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Peripheral nerves, connecting the central nervous system (CNS) to the rest of the body, are composed of axons covered by myelinating and non-myelinating Schwann cells (SC).
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: During neural development, axons are guided through embryonic tissues to reach their final targets.
source: During neural development, axons are guided through embryonic tissues to reach their final targets (Stoeckli, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoeckli, 2018.

claim: Secreted trophic factors ensure axonal survival until the connection is ultimately stabilized when the appropriate target is reached.
source: supported by secreted trophic factors ensuring axonal survival until the connection is ultimately stabilized when the appropriate target is reached (Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ye et al., 2019.

claim: Myelin sheaths are produced by Schwann cells wrapping larger axons in a 1:1 ratio to allow rapid saltatory conduction of action potentials.
source: Myelin sheaths are produced by SC wrapping larger axons in a 1:1 ratio to allow rapid saltatory conduction of action potentials.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about myelination.

claim: Non-myelinating Schwann cells associate with multiple small caliber axons to form Remak bundles without forming compact myelin sheaths.
source: Non-myelinating SC associate with multiple small caliber axons to form Remak bundles without forming compact myelin sheaths.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about non-myelinating Schwann cells.

claim: After transection, peripheral nerves can repair and reconnect and this process implicates migration of Schwann cells to guide regrowing axons.
source: In fact, after transection, peripheral nerves can repair and reconnect and this process implicates migration of SC to guide regrowing axons.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about nerve regeneration.

claim: At E16, no blood vessels were observed inside the sciatic nerve.
source: At E16, we noticed new blood vessels emerging from the aligned extrinsic artery to form a peri-nervous vascular plexus (Figure 1B, arrowhead). Developing from this latter, numerous angiogenic sprouts invade the inside part of the immature nerve, starting to form the intra-nervous vascular network (INV) as observed in the optical section of the proximal part of the nerve (Figure 1C, arrowhead). However, at E16, in the distal part no blood vessels were found inside the nerve (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing blood vessels in the proximal but not distal part at E16.

claim: Schwann cell precursors and immature Schwann cells provide trophic support for neurons allowing their survival and normal nerve fasciculation during development.
source: Nevertheless, during development, SCP (present around E13) and iSC (from E15 to P0) provide trophic support for neurons allowing their survival and normal nerve fasciculation (Fledrich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fledrich et al., 2019.

claim: In Krox20Cre/Fl mutant mice, Schwann cells blocked in immature stage and unmyelinating Schwann cells are present and are expected to support the metabolic demand of axons.
source: In Krox20Cre/Fl mutant mice, those cells are present (SC blocked in immature stage and unmyelinating SC which do not express Krox20) and are expected to support the metabolic demand of axons, as normal axonal density was found (Decker et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of immature and unmyelinating Schwann cells and supported by a citation to Decker et al., 2006.

claim: Compact myelin sheaths are dense structures composed of lipids.
source: Moreover, compact myelin sheaths are dense structures, composed of lipids (Salzer, 2015), and could have biophysical properties not favorable or less permissive to the migration and propagation of blood vessels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salzer, 2015.

claim: Compact myelin sheaths could have biophysical properties not favorable or less permissive to the migration and propagation of blood vessels.
source: Moreover, compact myelin sheaths are dense structures, composed of lipids (Salzer, 2015), and could have biophysical properties not favorable or less permissive to the migration and propagation of blood vessels.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the physical properties of myelin.

claim: The myelin environment could block the diffusion of pro-angiogenic factors produced by other cells in the nerve such as vascular endothelial growth factor expressed by neurons.
source: This environment could also block the diffusion of pro-angiogenic factors produced by other cells in the nerve such as vascular endothelial growth factor expressed by neurons (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: Around E16 when immature Schwann cells proliferate, INV starts to develop.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that different stages of SC development orchestrate the INV formation: around E16 when the immature SC proliferate, INV starts to develop.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal correlation between immature Schwann cell proliferation and INV onset.

claim: Between P0 and P10, when myelination is happening, INV density decreases but maturation occurs.
source: Between P0 and P10, when myelination is happening, INV density decreases but maturation occurs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing decreased vascular density and increased maturation markers during this period.

claim: The anti-angiogenic effect of glial cells in the PNS appears to be the opposite in the CNS.
source: This anti-angiogenic effect of the glial cells appears to be the opposite in the CNS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison with CNS data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Guidance molecules controlling angiogenesis in different systems during embryogenesis are reported.
source: Guidance molecules controlling angiogenesis in different systems during embryogenesis are reported (Michaelis, 2014) but the molecular control of INV formation is not well known.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Michaelis, 2014.

claim: The molecular control of INV formation is not well known.
source: Guidance molecules controlling angiogenesis in different systems during embryogenesis are reported (Michaelis, 2014) but the molecular control of INV formation is not well known.
evidence: This claim is based on the lack of prior knowledge in the field.

claim: The molecular couple Netrin-1/UNC5B is involved in INV establishment.
source: This point out that the molecular couple Netrin-1/UNC5B is involved in INV establishment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of Netrin-1 and UNC5B loss of function on INV.

claim: INV and Schwann cells/myelin could be linked not only during development but also during peripheral nerve disease progression.
source: Our study opens the exciting possibility that INV and SC/myelin could be linked not only during development but also during peripheral nerve diseases progression.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from developmental findings to disease contexts.

claim: INV implication in demyelinating diseases should not be overlooked.
source: Thus, INV implication in demyelinating diseases should not be overlooked.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting future research directions.
